I had a great chat with my friend @jacalulu (PM Director at Google Labs) about how Gemini 4 changed how Google builds products and how parents can get kids to explore AI. Some takes I loved: 1. “It shouldn’t take someone longer to read your doc than it took you to write it.” Writing is thinking. AI can be a thought partner, but you should firmly be in the driver’s seat. 2. “It’s no longer about can you build it, it’s about should it even exist?” Code went from a scarce asset to basically free. If you can “throw a couple of agents at it over a weekend,” it’s probably not a durable product. So the hard part now is deciding what’s worth building in the first place. 3. “Why do you even want a person in your product?” Agents do more of our work every month, so you should ask if your product needs a UI at all. Jaclyn thinks people will still show up to create, learn, or be entertained. Any task that feels like a chore should be built for agents first. 4. “Don’t just give users exactly what they want.” Talk to them all the time, but find the root problem and solve it in a way they wouldn’t have thought of. You want them to walk away thinking, “I didn’t think this was possible, but it’s exactly what I wanted.” 5. “You shouldn’t expect users to know how to write elaborate prompts.” Small business owners don’t have time to start from an empty prompt box. So her team built Pomelli, Google’s tool for SMBs to create on-brand content, to read your website and learn your business first. 6. “Let your kid be your creative director.” Jaclyn’s 5-year-old loves scary stories, so they made their own podcast, Maya and the Fog. Her daughter picks the voices, names the characters, and gives notes on each cut, and Jaclyn has the agent produce the episode.
